title: The ImmigrationOS Contract: One Platform, Two Paymasters, and the Machinery of Removal

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Palantir's data-integration contracts capture fees at every layer of the enforcement stack — analysis, targeting, and case management — so that every intensification of enforcement activity, whatever its policy outcome, is billable platform revenue.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The revolving-door structure is the compromise: the same vendor serves the Pentagon's targeting stack (the cited Maven Smart System, SETAF, and APAS task orders) and ICE's immigration enforcement, so the tools of warfighting arrive in domestic policing pre-funded by defense contracts and pre-cleared by defense procurement.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The immigration system's data layer is closed to the public: ICE's caseload, targeting rules, and Palantir's role in generating them are proprietary or classified-adjacent, and the 2025 policy wave was reported as politics while its contract plumbing — the DOD IDIQ the task orders hang on — stayed in procurement databases.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: Since ICE's 2014 ICANTS system, Palantir has converted agency dependence into lock-in; the ImmigrationOS contract — reported near $30 million by public reporting, not by these ledger rows — extends the monopoly to the core enforcement mission itself.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: No inquiry has examined the platform's role in removal operations; oversight of the contract defaults to procurement audits while the policy debate treats the machinery as neutral infrastructure, and the platform's contribution to outcomes remains unexamined by any body.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The ImmigrationOS contract inherited the post-9/11 security-contracting economy and Palantir's own In-Q-Tel-incubated franchise — intelligence community seed capital, defense-procurement channels, and the enforcement-agency customer base built on them.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The contract institutionalizes the dual-use platform across the enforcement state: one integration layer spanning warfighting and removal, with defense contracts funding capabilities that domestic agencies deploy.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Defense task orders and immigration contracts recirculate to the same balance sheet — the platform's growth in one domain lowers the cost of its deployment in the other, and shareholders capture both while bearing neither mission's accountability.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: The ImmigrationOS contract completes the arc this atlas tracks from Team Themis: the surveillance proposal of 2011, priced for corporate clients, matures into standing public infrastructure for enforcement — the machinery that future crises of state capacity will call upon.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: The partisan-outrage cycle — ICE raids as pure politics, Palantir as pure villain — that treats the contract as an aberration of one administration's immigration policy.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The partisan frame erases the structure: the ICE relationship is a decade old (ICANTS, 2014), the platform spans administrations, and the contract's significance is the durable fusion of defense procurement and domestic enforcement under one vendor — a structure no election alters.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: This dossier marks the distinction: the cited rows are the documented federal award ledger — Palantir USG's Department of Defense IDIQ task orders (W91QVN26FA191, W912CM26FA001, W912CM26FA008, W912CM25FA021 and related) and the 2026 SEC filing record — while the ICE ImmigrationOS contract itself is established by public reporting (reported near $30 million, 2022), not by these ledger rows; the closed-loop structure is the documented mechanism.
